summary: Intro demo focused on multi-tenant rate fencing, org/project key strategies and handling bursty payments-like traffic. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated with strong security requirements. SE showed console flows for org keys, burst quotas, fairshare, and sticky routing; discussed fallback to lower-cost variants and KV/prefix caching implications. Agreed to run a scoped POC to validate 99th latency under mixed traffic and to share pricing options.

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood Inference. we got Jonah our systems engineer and Priya on product, um we'll run through rate-fencing patterns and then open for Q&A.
[00:14] Aisha: afternoon, thanks. traffic is kinda spiky for us, we have a payments notifications pipeline that has big bursts during settlement windows. we're trying to figure out how to prevent noisy tenants from chewing up our tokens.
[00:28] Jonah (SE): yeah and that's exactly where org/project keying helps. we'll show two topologies: single org key with per-project metadata, and dedicated project keys mapped to quotas. each has tradeoffs for billing and routing.
[00:41] Luis (SRE): quick Q, is the billing then per-project key? we want per-customer chargeback.
[00:47] Maya: yes you can map billing to project keys so accounting is clean. if you use org-wildcard keys you can still do tag-based usage but it's trickier for invoice line-iteming.
[01:02] Jonah: starting demo, pulling up Console -> Governance -> Key topology. this view shows active tokens, associated projects, and current concurrency slices. note that the console has a live QPS heatmap, and you can set soft/hard quotas.
[01:18] [screen share noise] Jonah: here I'm configuring a "burst fence" policy. the idea: each key gets a base rate, a burst bucket, and a cooldown window. when a key hits hard limit we can either queue, drop, or route to a cheaper model variant as a fallback.
[01:33] Ben (Security): about the fallback to cheaper variants — are we sure that's safe for PII? we can't degrade to a public model for regulated traffic.
[01:43] Priya (Product): great point. policies can be annotated with data classification. you can configure policy rules to never fallback for keys marked PHI, and those keys can be pinned to Dedicated or Private deployments.
[01:57] Nora (CTO): timeline question — our procurement needs to know if Dedicated is required for compliant PII handling or if hosted with VPC+KMS will suffice.
[02:08] Maya: depends on control plane expectations. many customers use Hosted + VPC peering + customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest and are SOC2 happy, but some prefer Dedicated for stronger tenancy isolation. we'll add a comparison doc.
[02:22] Jonah: back to live traffic — here's a sample rule I'm simulating: fairshare across projects, with a reservation of 20% capacity for gold tenants then best-effort for others. see the graph — under heavy spike, gold stays within SLO, others throttle.
[02:40] Aisha: can we set preemptive throttles for a tenant before they cross the threshold? like soft limits that warn then hard limit?
[02:47] Jonah: yes soft alerts, then automated throttling. soft is metric-based alert with webhook, and the system supports gradual ramp-down policies so you don't see sharp failures.
[02:58] Luis: what about backpressure to our clients? any recommended client-side patterns?
[03:03] Jonah: yes recommended patterns: client should implement exponential retry with jitter, observe Retry-After header, and use sticky routing keys to maintain KV cache locality. KV caching reduces per-token compute for repeated contexts.
[03:20] Aisha: sticky routing, can you expand? is that per-project key pinned to a pool?
[03:25] Jonah: exactly. when you pin a project key to a pool, subsequent requests hit the same serving nodes which preserves KV cache and lowers p95/p99 latency. downside is less global load balance and possible hotspots; we expose pool-level autoscaling to mitigate.
[03:42] Priya: and we have a sticky-aware scheduler that moves warm state proactively during planned outages.
[03:49] [small crosstalk, typing]
[04:02] Maya: let's talk about unit economics quickly — batching, prefix KV caching and quantization all reduce per-token cost. Jonah did a quick numbers calc for a chat workload — enabling KV cache cut per-token cost by ~18% in our last benchmark.
[04:18] Jonah: the catch is cold starts for new routing keys — first request pays warmup. so our burst buckets and warmup TTL settings are important.
[04:28] Nora: curious about SLO verification — can you run a benchmark that simulates our peaks and show 99th latency?
[04:35] Jonah: yes we can. that's one of the POC items — we'll run a simulated arrival model with your traffic curves. please share the curves.
[04:44] Aisha: we'll export a week with per-minute QPS and 95th/99th token lengths.
[04:49] Ben: security — how are audit logs produced, retention, and encryption? also SSO and RBAC?
[04:56] Priya: audit logs are streamed to your S3 or GCS with AES-256 and tie into customer KMS; retention is configurable. we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and RBAC roles at org/project levels.
[05:09] Ben: any certifications for the hosted environment?
[05:12] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II; we can share the report under NDA. Dedicated/private deployments have additional contractual controls.
[05:22] Luis: what about multiregion failover for low-latency routing? we can't tolerate 200ms spikes for EU customers.
[05:28] Jonah: routing policies support region preference and geo-failover. you can define latency SLOs per customer and the smart router will pick nearest healthy pool.
[05:40] Aisha: okay demo makes sense, show me one more: how do we quickly revoke a compromised key and re-route traffic?
[05:46] Jonah: revocation is a one-click in Console -> Keys -> Revoke; you can also rotate keys via API. after revocation, you can optionally create a temporary fallback key mapped to a different pool to drain state.
[05:59] [sound of a message ping]
[06:05] Nora (joined): sorry, timezone mix up, jumped in. quick Q: if a tenant is on Dedicated but occasionally wants to burst to Hosted, do you support hybrid routing?
[06:15] Maya: yes hybrid is supported via policy-based routing; you can allow overflow to a hosted pool when dedicated is saturated with data-compliance annotations preventing PHI from overflowing.
[06:29] Maya: recap: we showed topologies, burst fences, sticky routing, and fallback policies; action items are benchmark run, pricing deck, and security pack.
[06:38] Aisha: sounds good. any blockers on Redwood side?
[06:41] Maya: we need your traffic curves and list of keys that will be PHI-bound. Jonah will draft the benchmark plan.
[06:48] Luis: one last question on observability — can we get token-level tracing and costs per trace?
[06:54] Priya: yep token-level cost breakdown per request is available, plus trace IDs you can join to your APM, and per-route dashboards.
[07:05] Maya: excellent okay we'll follow up with the POC scoping invite for 06/02 and share the docs. thanks all.
[07:12] [meeting ends]
